newsitem.title: UK: LME copper nudges $2,170 resistance in thin trade.
newsitem.headline: LME copper nudges $2,170 resistance in thin trade.

text.p: Copper prices shot up on Thursday to probe the key $2,170 resistance level, while its stable mates on the London Metal Exchange (LME) made steady upside progress.
Light buying attributed to commission houses exaggerated price movements amid low volumes in a market still in the grips of the year-end holiday lull, dealers said.
Three-months copper ended the afternoon kerb at the day's high of $2,167 a tonne, a gain of $40 from Tuesday, the last time the market was open, and the high since December 20.
Early in the day, prices had drifted down from strong opening levels just under $2,150 to a low of $2,131 before whipping higher in ring trading.
Cash/threes backwardation also widened by $15 to about $110.
"Commission houses were using the thin conditions to juggle the market to their own advantage. There was very little business to be seen today," a trader said.
"It's very easy to bully the price under such thin conditions," another added.
Above the $2,170-$2,175 resistance area, copper prices were susceptible to further gains towards $2,200, analysts said.
However, the LME stocks report would set the tone for the market on Friday, with some traders expecting a moderate rise.
The January 1997 options declaration on copper passed quietly with $2,200 copper calls declared and puts at the same strike price abandoned, options dealers said.
January aluminium prices held above $1,500 by the time of the declaration, meaning significant open interest on puts at that strike was not activated.
But aluminium followed copper higher to finish the kerb $9 firmer at $1,555, also at the day's highs.

Lead rallied from a low of $694 to finish stronger at $707. Values were initially boosted by the option declaration as $700 calls were declared despite the fact that the market was slightly below the strike at the declaration deadline.
This led to short-covering from option market makers, sparking a small rally, options traders said.
Later in the day news that the Nordenham lead plant in Germany was halted for repairs until late January helped cement lead's gains.
Nickel also moved smartly higher, on the path to recovery from Monday's drop to fresh 2-1/4 lows. It finished the kerb at $6,595, a gain of $130.
Alloy firmed to $1,425, a gain to $25, while zinc edged up $2 to $1,062.
But tin bucked the trend to end $20 lower at $5,820, after Far Eastern selling emerged at $5,840, dealers said.
